hook.support: Have you heard a talk that went everywhere and nowhere? You got lost. A plan fixes that. Start, middle, end. With signs along the way.
hook.core: You’ve sat through a talk that wandered: no clear point, no idea where it was going, no ending. Listeners can’t scroll back up. They need you to tell them where you’re going, take them there step by step, and tell them when you’ve arrived.
hook.extend: Listeners can’t reread. A spoken text has to carry its own map: a clear opening, a small number of connected points, and an ending that pulls it together, with signposts that show how each idea links to the next.

why.support: A plan helps people follow you. It helps you not get lost too.
why.core: Any time you speak at work, in class or at a meeting, a clear plan makes you easier to follow and easier to remember.
why.extend: Structuring oral content is a core skill for presentations, briefings, interviews and meetings. It’s what makes advice usable.

articles.title: A map for your listeners

body.support:
When you read, you can go back. When you listen, you can’t. So a talk needs a clear plan.

**A good plan:**
- **Hook:** grab attention. Ask a question. Tell a short story.
- **Say what’s coming:** “I’ll tell you three things.”.
- **Main points:** two or three. Not ten.
- **Wrap-up:** say your points again in one or two lines. End strong.
.
**Put your points in order.** You could go:
- from first to last (time order).
- from smallest to biggest.
- from problem to fix.

**Use signposts.** A **signpost** is a word that shows where your talk is going.
- To start a point: “First…” “Next…”.
- To link ideas: “So…” “Because of that…”.
- To finish: “To sum up…”.

**Use cue cards.** Write a few key words on each card. Don’t write the whole talk.
body.core:
Readers can go back a page. Listeners can’t. That’s why a talk needs a stronger structure than writing, and why good speakers keep telling the audience where they are.

**The structure:**
- **Hook:** a question, a surprising fact or a short story.
- **Preview:** tell them what’s coming. “I’m going to cover three things: cost, safety and time.”.
- **Main points:** two or three. Each with one example or piece of evidence.
- **Wrap-up:** sum up the points, and end with a strong final line or a call to action.
.
**Sequence your points.** Choose an order that makes sense for your topic:
- **time order:** first, then, finally.
- **problem → solution**.
- **least to most important:** save your best point for last.
- **simple to complex:** build up.

**Signpost every move.** **Signposts** are words that show how ideas connect. They help listeners keep up.
- **Starting a point:** “First…”, “My second point is…”, “Finally…”.
- **Adding:** “Also…”, “On top of that…”.
- **Cause and effect:** “Because of this…”, “That’s why…”.
- **Contrast:** “But…”, “On the other hand…”.
- **Wrapping up:** “So, to sum up…”, “The one thing to remember is…”.

**Cue cards.** One card per section. Key words only, in big writing, numbered in order.
body.extend:
Spoken texts are processed in real time. Listeners cannot reread, so a talk needs a more explicit structure than writing, with frequent signals about where it is and where it is going.

**Structure.**
- **hook:** a question, statistic, anecdote or bold claim.
- **preview:** an outline of the main points, so listeners know the shape.
- **body:** usually two to four main points, each developed with an example or evidence.
- **wrap-up:** a summary and a memorable close, often a call to action or a return to the hook.

**Sequencing.** Choose an organising principle to suit the purpose: chronological; problem–solution; cause–effect; or least to most important, ending on your strongest point.

**Signalling connections.** **Signposts** and **transitions** are the spoken equivalent of headings and paragraphs:
- **enumerating:** first, second, finally.
- **adding:** in addition, also, what’s more.
- **cause and effect:** as a result, which means, that’s why.
- **contrast:** however, on the other hand, but.
- **summing up:** to sum up, the key point is.

Repetition is a feature, not a fault. Restating your points in the wrap-up helps listeners remember.

**Script and cue cards.** Writing a full script helps you check sentence structure, punctuation and flow. Then reduce it to cue cards with key words, so you speak rather than read.

caseStudies.title: Three stories

body.support:
In **2005**, **Steve Jobs** gave a speech to students at **Stanford University** in the US. He started Apple, the company that makes iPhones.

He began by saying what was coming. He said he would tell **three stories** from his life. That’s it. Just three.

Then he told them, one by one:
- **Story 1:** about joining the dots in your life.
- **Story 2:** about love and loss.
- **Story 3:** about death.
.
The plan was simple. Everyone knew where he was going.
body.core:
On **12 June 2005**, **Steve Jobs**, co-founder of Apple, gave the graduation speech at **Stanford University** in the US.

His structure was simple, and he told the audience exactly what it was. Near the start, he said he wanted to tell them **three stories** from his life. Nothing more.

Then he signposted each one clearly as he went:
- the **first** story was about connecting the dots: how small choices made sense later.
- the **second** was about love and loss: being fired from the company he started.
- the **third** was about death.

Each story ended with a lesson, and the speech closed with a short, memorable line.

The speech is about 15 minutes long. Because the structure was so clear, listeners always knew where they were.
body.extend:
On **12 June 2005**, Apple co-founder **Steve Jobs** delivered the commencement address at **Stanford University**.

Its structure is often used to teach speech planning. Early on, Jobs previewed it in plain words: he would tell **three stories** from his life. Nothing more. That preview set expectations and gave the audience a mental map.

Each story was then explicitly signposted (“the first story”, “my second story”, “my third story”) and each ended with a lesson that linked back to the speech’s overall theme:
- connecting the dots, and trusting that choices will make sense later.
- love and loss, including being fired from the company he co-founded.
- death, and how awareness of it shapes priorities.

The close returned to a single, repeated line.

Fortune has reported that the screenwriter Aaron Sorkin helped with the speech, though how much is disputed. Either way, the lesson is the same: a simple, explicit structure makes a talk easy to follow and remember.

model.text:
**Card 1, Hook + preview:** “Who’s eaten two-minute noodles three nights in a row?” Three tips: plan, shop, cook.
**Card 2, Point 1:** First: plan. Five meals. Write the list.
**Card 3, Point 2:** Next: shop. Stick to the list. Buy home brand.
**Card 4, Point 3:** Most importantly: cook. Big batch Sunday. Freeze it.
**Card 5, Wrap-up:** To sum up: plan, shop, cook. Your wallet will thank you.
why: Card 1 hooks and previews the three tips in one go.
Each card starts with a signpost: “First”, “Next”, “Most importantly”.
Only key words are written, so the speaker talks rather than reads.

rubric.great: A preview and a strong last line.
Signposts link ideas, not just list them.

teacher.overview: Students learn why talks need explicit structure (listeners can’t reread), plan a talk with a hook, preview, two or three sequenced points and a wrap-up, and use signposts and transitions to signal connections. They produce a plan and cue cards (extend: a script with correct conventions). The case study is Steve Jobs’ 2005 Stanford address, structured as three clearly previewed and signposted stories.
prep: Optional: the opening minute of the Stanford speech (widely available online) to hear the preview.

teacher.answers:
**Annotation:** 1 hook question; 2 preview of three reasons; 3 “first” signpost; 4 “on top of that” adds; 5 strongest point last (“finally, and most importantly”); 6 wrap-up repeats the points and ends with a call to action.

**Sort:** starts a point — first of all; my second point is. Links — because of that; on the other hand. Wraps up — to sum up; the one thing to remember is.

**Case study:** Jobs previewed “three stories”; signposted each as first, second, third; topics were connecting the dots, love and loss, and death; each ended with a lesson linked to the theme.

resources.label: Fortune — on the writing of the Stanford speech (2016)

realityCheck: **The third story is about death.** Jobs speaks about his cancer diagnosis. Preview it with students and be mindful of recent losses.
**The rambling-talk hook works best if it’s genuinely bad.** Students instantly see the value of structure.
**Cue cards beat scripts for delivery,** but writing a script first helps weaker writers check their ideas link.
**Works in a real class:** yes. It pairs directly with Nail the Delivery and the Speak Up presentation.

levels.support: Aimed at about Years 3–4 reading: shorter article and case study, 6 key words, word bank and two main points.
levels.core: Aimed at about Years 5–6 reading: the standard version with preview, sequencing, signposts and cue cards.
levels.extend: Aimed at about Year 7 and up: organising principles, transitions, purposeful repetition and a scripted draft.
